Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 2 Samuel 17:

---

## 2 Samuel 17 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Ahithophel's Plan
Ahithophel proposes an immediate, targeted strike: he himself will choose 12,000 men and pursue David that very night. Gill notes that Ahithophel took upon himself to be general of the army, not merely a counsellor—possibly so Absalom would stay behind and not be tempted to spare David out of residual affection. He wanted to act *that night* for surprise and speed. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

Ellicott observes that Ahithophel "saw clearly that Absalom's success depended on striking an immediate blow." David was weary and in no condition to resist. Yet Ellicott notes that from vv. 16 and 15:28, David was already encamped by the Jordan fords—a greater distance than one day's march from Jerusalem—so "this night" may not literally mean the night David left the city. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Precept Austin adds an important biographical note: Bathsheba's father was Eliam, who was the son of Ahithophel (2 Sam 23:34). That makes Ahithophel Bathsheba's *grandfather*. This may explain why a political counsellor—not a military man—was so eager to personally lead the attack against David: a possible motive of personal revenge for David's adultery with his granddaughter and murder of her husband. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-17-commentary)

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the plan one of "deep political sagacity" whose adoption "would have extinguished the cause of David." (https://ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb/jfb.x.x.xvii.html)

---

### v. 2 — "Strike Down Only the King"
Ahithophel would attack while David is "weary and weak-handed" (the Hebrew suggests hands dropping to the side from exhaustion), throw him into panic, and kill only David. Ellicott says the translation "will make him afraid" is too weak; the idea is throwing the whole band into a *panic* by a sudden night attack and securing the king's person in the confusion. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Precept Austin notes the repeated "I will" (four times across vv. 2–3) as evidence of Ahithophel's pride and egocentricity. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-17-commentary)

---

### v. 3 — "As a Bride Returning to Her Husband"
Ahithophel promises to bring all the people back to Absalom once David is dead. The BSB and ESV include the simile "as a bride returning to her husband." Ellicott calls this "artful flattery"—Ahithophel assumes Absalom is the rightful king and the people merely need to be brought back to their true allegiance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

The NET Bible note explains that the Hebrew text of this verse is difficult; the LXX reads differently, and modern translations divide—some following the Hebrew (NASB, NIV), others the LXX (NAB, NRSV, NLT). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-17-commentary)

Gill observes that Ahithophel speaks of David contemptuously ("the man whom thou seekest") and that Absalom clearly sought David's *life*, not just his throne. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 4 — Absalom and the Elders Approve
The plan pleased Absalom and all the elders. Gill finds it "strange" that the elders of Israel would so readily agree to the death of a prince who had ruled them with justice, fought their battles, and raised the nation to unprecedented glory. He attributes it to Absalom's ambition. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

Precept Austin notes that Ahithophel's advice was regarded "as if one inquired of the word of God" (2 Sam 16:23), and his preceding "concubine plan" had already been a success—so Absalom and the elders were predisposed to trust him. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-17-commentary)

---

### v. 5 — Absalom Calls for Hushai
Despite unanimous approval of Ahithophel's plan, Absalom unexpectedly summons Hushai. Gill calls this "very remarkable in the providence of God"—that Absalom would seek a second opinion from David's known friend, when Ahithophel was a sworn ally. He attributes it entirely to God's will to defeat Ahithophel's counsel and blind Absalom's mind. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) calls it "a remarkable evidence of the hand of God and answer to David's prayer in 2 Samuel 15:31." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

---

### v. 6 — Absalom Presents Ahithophel's Plan to Hushai
Absalom recounts Ahithophel's advice and asks, "Should we carry it out? If not, what do you say?" Gill notes that Absalom may have hoped Hushai would concur, thereby strengthening the original counsel, since "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 7 — "Not Good at This Time"
Hushai says: "This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound." Ellicott notes the word order in Hebrew suggests "This time the counsel of Ahithophel is not good"—implying that his *previous* advice (to defile David's concubines, 2 Sam 16:21) had been wise. This gave Hushai an appearance of candour and fairness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 8 — David's Men: "Like a Bear Robbed of Her Cubs"
Hushai paints David and his men as fierce, desperate warriors. Gill explains "chafed in their minds" (Hebrew: "bitter in soul") as meaning enraged and full of wrath—not depressed but *desperate*, fighting furiously because their wives, children, and estates are all at stake. The she-bear robbed of cubs was proverbial for uncontrollable fury (see Hosea 13:8). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

Guzik notes that Hushai spoke of the David *of the past*, not the present—he had seen David with his own eyes and knew he was not strong and mighty at that moment, but he hoped Absalom would vividly remember past David. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

---

### v. 9 — David Hiding in a Cave, and the Risk of an Initial Defeat
Hushai argues that David is hiding in a cave or pit (as he did when fleeing Saul) and that if Absalom's advance force suffers even a small casualty, the news will spread panic. Gill suggests David might even spring an ambush from hiding, causing a "slaughter among the people who follow Absalom." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 10 — "Even the Most Valiant Soldier with the Heart of a Lion Will Melt"
Hushai warns that even the bravest will lose heart if there is an initial reverse, "for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man." Gill discusses the lion as proverbial for courage (the Hebrew word *labi* for lion may derive from *leb*, "heart"), and mentions an alternate reading: some apply this to David himself—"shall *he* utterly melt?"—with the answer being no, he will not be so easily frightened. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 11 — Hushai's Counter-Plan: Gather All Israel
Hushai advises gathering "all Israel from Dan to Beersheba—a multitude like the sand on the seashore" and that Absalom personally lead them. Ellicott calls this a difficult rhetorical task—Hushai had to "make the worse appear the better reason" against a famously wise counsellor, while his own loyalty was suspect. He succeeded by "emphasising all the possible hazards" of Ahithophel's plan and proposing one that, with "delicate flattery," assumed all Israel was already on Absalom's side. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Guzik notes two key elements of the plan: (a) gathering all Israel would *take time*, buying David precious days; (b) suggesting Absalom lead in person flattered his vanity—Ahithophel's plan had Ahithophel leading; Hushai's plan had *Absalom* leading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

---

### v. 12 — "Like Dew on the Ground"
Hushai uses the image of dew falling—silent, pervasive, covering everything—to describe the overwhelming invasion. Gill notes the phrase expresses both numbers (countless drops) and irresistible force, coming secretly and opportunely. The Romans had a class of light-armed soldiers called *rorarii* ("dew-men") who fought first, because dew falls before rain. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 13 — "We Will Drag It Down to the Valley"
Hushai's hyperbole: if David retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes and drag the city into the river until not a pebble remains. Ellicott calls this "hyperbole to show the irresistible power of all Israel united … pleasing to the vanity and dazzling to the imagination of Absalom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Gill explains "ropes" may refer to scaling ropes, or to engines worked with ropes for demolishing cities, or may simply be a hyperbolic expression of easy demolition by sheer numbers. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 14 — The Lord's Sovereign Purpose
**The pivotal theological verse.** Absalom and all Israel declare Hushai's advice better. The narrator explains: "For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom."

Guzik offers three observations: (i) This was the first time anyone ever said Hushai's counsel was better than Ahithophel's. (ii) "Absalom had the smartest man in Israel on his side, but David's prayer was mightier than Ahithophel's intelligence." (iii) God was in control—He had earlier led Ahithophel to give *foolish* counsel that was followed (16:20-23), and now He caused *wise* counsel to be rejected. God's sovereignty overrules human wisdom. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Men cannot escape God. They go their own way, but that way never sets them free from the authority and the invincible power of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

Precept Austin and Gill both reference Proverbs 19:21: "Many are the plans in a man's heart, but the counsel of the LORD will stand." Gill says the Lord "blinded" the minds of Absalom and the elders. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### vv. 15–16 — Hushai Sends Warning to David
Hushai reports both plans to Zadok and Abiathar and urges them to send word to David: "Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but cross over." Ellicott notes Hushai's urgency—though his advice was accepted at the moment, it could easily be exchanged for Ahithophel's; David must put the Jordan between himself and the rebels without delay. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Hushai was "apparently doubting that his advice would be followed"—he sent the warning lest Ahithophel's influence might yet produce a change in Absalom's mind. (https://ccel.org/ccel/jamieson/jfb/jfb.x.x.xvii.html)

---

### v. 17 — The Spy Network at En-rogel
Jonathan and Ahimaaz (sons of the priests) wait at En-rogel, a fountain just outside Jerusalem. A servant girl relays messages. Ellicott locates En-rogel at either the "Fountain of the Virgin" on the Kidron slope or (more likely for the Joshua boundary description) "Job's Well" at the junction of Kidron and Hinnom valleys. Women regularly came to draw water, so communications could pass without attracting attention. The definite article suggests the "maid-servant" (*wench* in KJV) was a well-known servant of the high priest. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 18 — The Couriers Spotted; Escape to Bahurim
A young man sees them and reports to Absalom. They flee to Bahurim—the same village where Shimei had cursed David (2 Sam 16:5). They hide in a man's well in his courtyard. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

---

### v. 19 — The Woman Covers the Well with Grain
The man's wife spreads a covering over the well-mouth and scatters grain (ground corn, likely wheat or barley with hulls removed, spread to dry) over it, concealing the hiding place entirely. Ellicott says this word for "ground corn" occurs elsewhere only in Proverbs 27:22. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 20 — The Woman's Deception
When Absalom's servants ask for Ahimaaz and Jonathan, the woman says "They have crossed over the brook." The men search, find nothing, and return to Jerusalem. Ellicott compares this to Rahab hiding the spies (Joshua 2:4–7) and Michal deceiving Saul's messengers (1 Sam 19:12–17), noting "the historian simply records without comment what was done." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 21 — The Message Delivered
After the pursuers leave, the messengers climb out, reach David, and tell him: "Cross over the river at once, for Ahithophel has given this advice against you."

---

### v. 22 — David Crosses the Jordan
David and all his people cross the Jordan. By daybreak, not one remained on the west side. Guzik notes: "Because of this successful intelligence operation, David escaped the immediate danger from Absalom." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

---

### v. 23 — Ahithophel's Suicide
Ahithophel sees his counsel rejected, rides home to Giloh, sets his house in order, and hangs himself. He is buried in his father's tomb.

Multiple commentators agree: this was not merely wounded pride. Ellicott says Ahithophel "was shrewd enough to see that, with this delay, Absalom's rebellion would inevitably fail, and he himself be likely to come to a traitor's death." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

Barnes adds: "He is a memorable example of the impotence of worldly wisdom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/2_samuel/17.htm)

The Cambridge Bible notes this is "the first deliberate suicide on record" and was "prompted by mortification at the rejection of his counsel; by the chagrin of baffled ambition; by the conviction that now the rebellion would inevitably fail." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_samuel/17.htm)

**On suicide:** Guzik (Enduring Word) addresses it directly: "Suicide is a sin because it is self-murder and God commanded you shall not murder (Exodus 20:13). Yet suicide should not be regarded as an unforgivable sin. Anyone who does commit suicide has given in to the lies and deceptions of Satan, whose purpose is to kill and destroy (John 10:10)." He quotes Spurgeon at length, who calls Ahithophel's act "a strange mixture of discretion and desperation": "To put his house in order, showed that he was a prudent man; to hang himself, proved that he was a fool." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

The parallel to Judas Iscariot is widely noted. Precept Austin lists the similarities: both were trusted friends who betrayed; both sided with the enemy to plot the king's death; both hanged themselves. Psalm 41:9 ("even my close friend … has turned against me") refers first to Ahithophel but is applied to Judas in John 13:18. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-17-commentary)

---

### v. 24 — David at Mahanaim; Absalom Crosses the Jordan
David reaches Mahanaim (east of the Jordan), and Absalom crosses with all Israel. Ellicott notes that Mahanaim had been Ish-bosheth's capital (2 Sam 2:8)—the same reasons making it suitable then made it a good refuge and rallying point for David now. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 25 — Amasa Appointed Commander
Absalom appoints Amasa over the army instead of Joab (who went with David). Amasa was son of Ithra (or Jether) and Abigail, who was sister to Zeruiah (Joab's mother)—making Amasa Joab's cousin and David's nephew by marriage. Ellicott notes that in 1 Chronicles 2:17, Ithra is called "Jether the Ishmeelite"—"Israelite" in 2 Samuel 17:25 is probably a textual error for "Ishmaelite," as the LXX reads. The identity of "Nahash" (father of Abigail) is uncertain; it may be Jesse's wife's name or indicate that Abigail and Zeruiah were half-sisters to Jesse's sons. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### v. 26 — Camped in Gilead
Absalom and the Israelite army camp in the land of Gilead. Ellicott locates Gilead as the territory east of the Jordan between Moab (south) and Bashan (north). Mahanaim was within Gilead, though Absalom did not actually reach it before being defeated. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

### vv. 27–29 — Provisions from Loyal Supporters
Three men bring supplies to David at Mahanaim:
- **Shobi** son of Nahash, from Rabbah of the Ammonites—Ellicott suggests he may have been a brother of Hanun (the former Ammonite king whom David conquered), left as governor and now showing gratitude. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)
- **Machir** son of Ammiel from Lo-debar—the same man who had sheltered Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9:4). David's earlier kindness to Jonathan's crippled son is now repaid. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)
- **Barzillai** the Gileadite from Rogelim—who appears again in 2 Samuel 19:31–39.

They bring beds, basins, pottery, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep, and cheese. Guzik reflects: "These otherwise obscure men are given special mention because they helped David in a time of great need. Friends in need are friends indeed." He calls them "specially sent by God to comfort David in his affliction." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

**"Cheese of kine"** (v. 29 in some translations): Ellicott notes this is a word of uncertain meaning occurring only here—the English follows the Chaldee, Syriac, and Rabbinic interpretation as "cheese," but the Vulgate has "fat calves" and Theodotion "sucking calves." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/17.htm)

---

## Summary of Distinctive Views by Tradition

I was unable to complete searches for tradition-specific commentaries (Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox) or modern scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org) within the available search limit. However, within the sources examined, some distinct perspectives emerge:

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Emphasises prayer as the decisive factor—David's prayer in 15:31 is what moved God's hand to defeat Ahithophel's counsel. Also emphasises spiritual warfare: suicide is attributed to "the lies and deceptions of Satan, whose purpose is to kill and destroy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

- **Older Calvinistic Baptist (Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik):** Highlights the paradox of Ahithophel—prudent enough to set his house in order, foolish enough to hang himself. Focus on the soul: "Thousands set their houses in order, but destroy their souls." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-17/)

- **Reformed/Providence Emphasis (Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Precept Austin):** Strong emphasis on God's sovereign "appointment" (Gill says God "blinded" Absalom's mind) to defeat Ahithophel's counsel. Gill suggests Absalom's calling for Hushai "can only be ascribed to the will of God." This aligns with classic Reformed teaching on God's meticulous providence over human decisions. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/17.htm)

- **Catholic/Orthodox and Modern Scholarship:** Searches to newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, and bibleodyssey.org could not be completed within the available limit. These perspectives are therefore not included here.
